heading: Test occupancy and nightly rate together in an investment model
body:
A rental model can look resilient when occupancy and nightly rate are stressed separately. In a weaker season, both may fall at the same time. Test combined changes and preserve the difference between room revenue, platform receipts, and cash available after operating expenses and financing.

Build the room-revenue bridge

Use available nights multiplied by paid occupancy multiplied by average daily rate. For a fictional property available 365 nights, 60% occupancy and a $250 nightly rate produce $54,750 of room revenue. A downside case with 50% occupancy and a $225 rate produces about $41,063. That is roughly 25% less room revenue, before considering other charges and costs.

Do not assume expenses fall at the same rate. Some cleaning and consumable costs follow stays, but insurance, property taxes, financing, internet, and many maintenance commitments continue. Model variable and fixed costs separately. Check whether cleaning fees collected from guests actually cover the associated expense rather than treating the entire fee as profit.

Show the cash needed to hold through a weak period

Spread revenue and payments across months using evidence for the market and property type. A positive annual total can hide several months of negative cash. Include the initial furnishing, repairs, launch period, and owner reserve outside the purchase-price headline.

Write the conditions under which you would reject the investment, revise the price, or seek better information. The most useful sensitivity analysis changes a decision. These are illustrative calculations, not return estimates for a particular property. Confirm local use restrictions, insurance, financing, and operating assumptions before investing.
